title: Right song, right role: Streisand, Williams and Walker, Lionel's saxophone
summary: He argues that wrong songs and wrong casting hold performers back, citing Barbra Streisand, the reversal of Williams and Walker, and a player Vodery switched to saxophone.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: Like, I heard Barbra Streisand sing "Mon Homme". But, where it was, it was the wrong place for it, you know what I mean? And then, she was singing a song that wasn't very good for her, anyhow. For this reason. French people, Edith Piaf and all of them, they like to sing low. And [Streisand] she was too high. Like in, "Mon Homme", she has a nice beautiful voice, but that was a question of the wrong song, what I'm trying to bring out.

You can give them the wrong song, and a person has the wrong tune, and they wonder why they're not a success. It's because they're not giving -- because, do you know, at one time, the great act of Williams and Walker // Williams was the straight man, he was a better looking man than Walker. George Walker was the comedian. And, then, suddenly, some fellow that knew them, like in the show business, turned around and said, "Look, you fellows are hooked up wrong. Why don't you turn it around, and then let Bert Williams do the comedy and then put cork on, and George Walker, you be straight." Because they had it around the wrong way.

Now, that was the greatest team we had. We've ever had. Bert Williams and George Walker. And they turned it around, they went over there, they had a Command Performance for the Queen of England. And he had diamonds, they gave him diamonds and everything.
But, before that, they didn't go no place. They couldn't even get in the Rabbit's Foot Minstrels (unintelligible).

They couldn't do nothing. But they were hooked wrong, you see? And, I know in the Army once ~~Strug~~ gling -- we had a fellow struggling around there - a fellow named Lionel. He was struggling around there with trying to play trombone. Wasn't going no place. He was a pianist, had been a church organist, you see. And they had switched him --

Bill Vodery had switched him to the saxophone, and in four or five days, he was playing the saxophone. And he was fooling around there with the trombone. I mean, you can get there in the wrong place, you know what I mean?
